chunks: From him, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Aban, from one who informed him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The gift (nuhlah) and the grant (hibah) are [valid] as long as possession has not been taken until the owner dies. He said: 'It is in the position of inheritance, and if the child is in his guardianship, it is valid.'

He said: And I asked him: Is it permissible for anyone to take back his gift and charity? He said: 'If he gives charity for the sake of Allah, then no. As for the gift (nuhlah) and the grant (hibah), he may take it back whether he has taken possession or not, even if it was for a relative.'

key_terms.النُّحْلُ: Gift or grant, often implying a specific type of gift distinct from general charity.
key_terms.الْمِيرَاثِ: Inheritance, used here to describe the status of the gift before death.
key_terms.الْهَبَةُ: Grant or gift, a general term for giving property.

ai.seo_question: Can a person revoke a gift they gave to their child or relative in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that while general charity (sadaqah) is irrevocable, gifts (hibah) and grants (nuhlah) remain revocable by the donor even after possession, a ruling that extends to children under guardianship. This distinction highlights the Shia jurisprudential view that the transfer of ownership in gifts is not final until the specific conditions of revocation are met, preserving the donor's right to retract unless explicitly waived.
